c01.display: Welcome back to NLP, Simply Explained. This is unit 1, lesson 2: tokenization.
c01.spoken: Welcome back to N L P, Simply Explained. This is unit 1, lesson 2: tokenization.

c02.display: Last time we climbed the staircase of NLP. Today we stand on the very first step, and look closely at how text gets cut into pieces.
c02.spoken: Last time we climbed the staircase of N L P. Today we stand on the very first step, and look closely at how text gets cut into pieces.

c03.display: Here is the idea to hold on to. A model never reads text the way you do. It reads tokens.
c03.spoken: Here is the idea to hold on to. A model never reads text the way you do. It reads tokens.

c04.display: So what is a token? A token is one unit of text that a model works with. It can be a whole word, a piece of a word, or a punctuation mark.
c04.spoken: So what is a token? A token is one unit of text that a model works with. It can be a whole word, a piece of a word, or a punctuation mark.

c05.display: Take the sentence "I don't like rain!" A typical tokenizer cuts it into six tokens: I, do, n't, like, rain, and the exclamation mark.
c05.spoken: Take the sentence "I don't like rain!" A typical tokenizer cuts it into six tokens: I, do, n apostrophe t, like, rain, and the exclamation mark.

c06.display: Think of it like chopping vegetables before you cook. You can't cook a whole pumpkin in one go, and the size you cut the pieces into changes everything.
c06.spoken: Think of it like chopping vegetables before you cook. You can't cook a whole pumpkin in one go, and the size you cut the pieces into changes everything.

c07.display: The obvious first idea is to split the text wherever there is a space. Let's see where that goes wrong.
c07.spoken: The obvious first idea is to split the text wherever there is a space. Let's see where that goes wrong.

c08.display: "traffic" with an exclamation mark stays glued together, so the punctuation becomes part of the word.
c08.spoken: "traffic" with an exclamation mark stays glued together, so the punctuation becomes part of the word.

c09.display: "don't" stays as one piece, even though it really means two words: do and not.
c09.spoken: "don't" stays as one piece, even though it really means two words: do and not.

c10.display: In "Doctor Rao", the dot after "Dr" does not end a sentence, but a simple splitter can't tell.
c10.spoken: In "Doctor Rao", the dot after "Dr" does not end a sentence, but a simple splitter can't tell.

c11.display: And "New York" is one name, but splitting on spaces breaks it into two unrelated words.
c11.spoken: And "New York" is one name, but splitting on spaces breaks it into two unrelated words.

c12.display: Fixing those cases with rules helps, but there is a bigger question: how big should a piece be? Let's cut the word "raindrops" three ways.
c12.spoken: Fixing those cases with rules helps, but there is a bigger question: how big should a piece be? Let's cut the word "raindrops" three ways.

c13.display: Option one: single characters. The vocabulary is tiny, and nothing is ever unknown. But every sentence turns into a very long sequence of letters.
c13.spoken: Option one: single characters. The vocabulary is tiny, and nothing is ever unknown. But every sentence turns into a very long sequence of letters.

c14.display: Option two: whole words. Each piece has meaning, but there are millions of words, names and typos. Any word missing from the list becomes "unknown".
c14.spoken: Option two: whole words. Each piece has meaning, but there are millions of words, names and typos. Any word missing from the list becomes "unknown".

c15.display: Option three: subwords. "raindrops" becomes "rain" plus "drops". Common words stay whole, and rare words are built from smaller pieces. That balance is why modern models use subwords.
c15.spoken: Option three: subwords. "raindrops" becomes "rain" plus "drops". Common words stay whole, and rare words are built from smaller pieces. That balance is why modern models use subwords.

c16.display: The most popular way to build a subword vocabulary is called Byte Pair Encoding, or BPE. It has just four steps.
c16.spoken: The most popular way to build a subword vocabulary is called Byte Pair Encoding, or BPE. It has just four steps.

c17.display: Split: start by breaking every word into single characters.
c17.spoken: Split: start by breaking every word into single characters.

c18.display: Count: count how often each pair of neighbouring pieces appears.
c18.spoken: Count: count how often each pair of neighbouring pieces appears.

c19.display: Merge: glue the most common pair together into a new piece.
c19.spoken: Merge: glue the most common pair together into a new piece.

c20.display: Repeat: count again and merge again, until the vocabulary is as big as you want.
c20.spoken: Repeat: count again and merge again, until the vocabulary is as big as you want.

c21.display: Let's try it on a tiny example. Our text contains "rain" nine times, "rainy" four times, "raining" five times and "train" three times.
c21.spoken: Let's try it on a tiny example. Our text contains "rain" nine times, "rainy" four times, "raining" five times and "train" three times.

c22.display: The most common pair is "i" followed by "n": twenty-six times, because "raining" contains it twice. So "i" and "n" merge into "in".
c22.spoken: The most common pair is "i" followed by "n": twenty-six times, because "raining" contains it twice. So "i" and "n" merge into "in".

c23.display: Next, "r" followed by "a" appears twenty-one times, so it becomes "ra".
c23.spoken: Next, "r" followed by "a" appears twenty-one times, so it becomes "ra".

c24.display: Then "ra" and "in" merge into "rain". After just three merges, the whole word "rain" is a single token.
c24.spoken: Then "ra" and "in" merge into "rain". After just three merges, the whole word "rain" is a single token.

c25.display: Now compare how many pieces each approach needs for "raindrops".
c25.spoken: Now compare how many pieces each approach needs for "raindrops".

c26.display: As characters, it is nine tokens: long, and each letter means very little.
c26.spoken: As characters, it is nine tokens: long, and each letter means very little.

c27.display: As subwords, it is just two: "rain" and "drops".
c27.spoken: As subwords, it is just two: "rain" and "drops".

c28.display: As a whole word, it is one, but only if "raindrops" happens to be in the vocabulary. Subwords give short sequences, with no unknown words.
c28.spoken: As a whole word, it is one, but only if "raindrops" happens to be in the vocabulary. Subwords give short sequences, with no unknown words.

c29.display: Time for a quick quiz. A subword tokenizer meets the word "unfriendliness" for the first time. What happens?
c29.spoken: Time for a quick quiz. A subword tokenizer meets the word "unfriendliness" for the first time. What happens?

c30.display: Pause the video and choose. Does it mark the word as unknown, split it into known pieces, or skip it?
c30.spoken: Pause the video and choose. Does it mark the word as unknown, split it into known pieces, or skip it?

c31.display: It splits it into known pieces: un, friend, li, ness. Pieces it has seen many times before.
c31.spoken: It splits it into known pieces: un, friend, li, ness. Pieces it has seen many times before.

c32.display: Let's recap. A token is one unit of text that a model reads.
c32.spoken: Let's recap. A token is one unit of text that a model reads.

c33.display: Splitting on spaces alone is not enough: punctuation, contractions and names get in the way.
c33.spoken: Splitting on spaces alone is not enough: punctuation, contractions and names get in the way.

c34.display: Subwords balance the two extremes: shorter than characters, and never unknown like whole words.
c34.spoken: Subwords balance the two extremes: shorter than characters, and never unknown like whole words.

c35.display: And BPE builds that vocabulary in four steps: split, count, merge, repeat.
c35.spoken: And BPE builds that vocabulary in four steps: split, count, merge, repeat.

c36.spoken: Next lesson: Text Classification. How does a spam filter decide?
